CONTESTED DIRECTOR ELECTIONS — COURT DETERMINATION OF THE VALIDITY OF AN ELECTION OR APPOINTMENT (CORP. CODE §§ 709, 305(C), 600(C), 601, 5617, 7616; CODE CIV. PROC. §§ 389, 803; LAWRENCE V. I. N. PARLIER ESTATE CO.; COLUMBIA ENGINEERING CO. V. JOINER; SHAHIN V. WAWRO; SPENCER V. OLDER; HAAH V. KIM; MORRICAL V. ROGERS) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jane Doe, states what California law provides when the result of a corporate election is disputed — when two rival groups each claim to be the board, when a shareholder says a meeting was never properly noticed, when shares were voted by someone whose right to vote is contested, or when directors were appointed rather than elected and someone questions the appointment. The central statute is Corporations Code section 709, which directs the superior court to try and determine the validity of an election or appointment of a director in an expedited proceeding, and which sits alongside the statutes that let a court order a shareholders' meeting to be held. The sheet describes who may file such an action, how quickly it is heard, what the court may decide and order, what the published decisions have held about the grounds that may be raised and the matters that may not, and the parallel provisions that apply to nonprofit corporations. Where a specific business name appears below, that is Acme, Inc.; this sheet can also be read on its own, without it filled in, as a general reference to what these statutes and decisions say. It states the law. It does not evaluate whether any particular election was valid, whether any person holds office as a director, whether any person has standing, or what any court would decide, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

WHO MAY FILE, WHICH CORPORATIONS ARE COVERED, AND WHERE THE ACTION IS FILED
Corporations Code § 709(a) creates a civil action to test a contested board seat. Two categories of plaintiff are named: any shareholder, and any person who claims to have been denied the right to vote. The court's mandate is stated in the imperative — the superior court of the proper county “shall try and determine” the validity of any election or appointment of any director. The statute reaches every domestic corporation, and it reaches a foreign corporation as well, but only where the election was held or the appointment was made in this state. For a foreign corporation the same subdivision fixes venue at the plaintiff's option: either the county of the corporation's principal California office, or the county where the election was held or the appointment was made. The statute covers appointments as well as elections, so a directorship filled by board action rather than by a shareholder vote is within it. The section as it now reads was last amended in 2022 (Stats. 2022, ch. 617, § 17).

THE FIVE-DAY HEARING DATE, SERVICE, AND WHAT COURTS HAVE SAID ABOUT ITS SPEED
Section 709(b) puts the proceeding on a short clock. On the filing of the complaint, and before any further proceedings are had, the court is to enter an order that fixes a hearing date within five days unless a later date is fixed for good cause shown, and that requires notice of the hearing date and a copy of the complaint to be served on the corporation, on the person whose purported election or appointment is questioned, and on any person other than the plaintiff whom the plaintiff alleges to have been elected or appointed; service is made as a summons is served, or by registered mail if the court so directs, and the court may impose further notice requirements as the circumstances make proper. In Morrical v. Rogers the Court of Appeal rejected the argument that this compressed schedule confines the statute to simple disputes or makes it unconstitutional to try complicated ones under it. The court read the phrase “before any further proceedings are had” as an indication that the hearing fixed by subdivision (b) is not necessarily the full trial of the complaint, and pointed out that the “good cause” clause allows a later date. In that case the complaint was filed in May 2012, the initial hearing was set for late June, and trial was held over seven days in June and July. The same opinion acknowledged that a summary trial of complex issues, conducted without the discovery and preparation available in an ordinary civil action, could deny a party procedural rights and due process.

WHAT THE COURT MAY DECIDE AND ORDER
Section 709(c) lists what the court may do. It may determine the person entitled to the office of director. It may order a new election to be held or an appointment to be made. It may determine the validity, effectiveness and construction of voting agreements and voting trusts, the validity of the issuance of shares, and the right of persons to vote. And it may direct such other relief as may be just and proper. Morrical v. Rogers read that subdivision as addressing the relief a court may direct rather than the grounds on which an election may be attacked, describing the list as nonexhaustive and the final phrase as a savings clause. Haah v. Kim described the breadth of the inquiry in similar terms, noting that courts deciding these actions have wide discretion to consider all matters relevant to the determination and are not limited by technical or procedural issues.

AN EQUITABLE PROCEEDING MEANT TO REPLACE QUO WARRANTO
The decisions describe the section 709 action as equitable and as a deliberate substitute for the older remedy of quo warranto. In Lawrence v. I. N. Parlier Estate Co., decided under the predecessor provision in Civil Code section 315, the California Supreme Court said the action is in the nature of an equitable proceeding in which the court will consider all matters necessary to a proper determination of the validity of the contested election and to a just direction of the relief required. Shahin v. Wawro explained the purpose of the statute in the same terms the earlier cases had used — that courts might have power to proceed in a summary manner to test the title of directors to office without recourse to the slow and cumbersome proceeding of quo warranto — and added that the section is available to a person seeking to uphold an election as well as to one seeking to overturn it. Morrical v. Rogers stated that section 709 and its predecessor statutes afford an equitable cause of action. Quo warranto itself survives in California as Code of Civil Procedure section 803, which authorizes an action brought by the Attorney General, in the name of the people, against a person who usurps, intrudes into, or unlawfully holds or exercises a public office or a franchise, or against a corporation that does so.

THE GROUNDS ON WHICH AN ELECTION MAY BE ATTACKED
Whether a section 709 action is confined to mechanical objections — notice, quorum, vote counting — or may rest on a claim that those who controlled the vote breached their duties was the central question in Morrical v. Rogers. A minority shareholder challenged the election of new directors on the ground that her brothers, who held the controlling shares, had material financial interests in the transactions the election implemented, and the Court of Appeal held that such grounds are available: after reviewing the statute's text, its place in the code, its legislative history, and the case law, the court concluded that section 709 permits a corporate electoral challenge on those grounds. It found nothing in the plain language restricting the grounds of challenge, observed that the standing sentence of subdivision (a) limits who may sue and says nothing about the grounds, and summed up that it would not infer an unwritten limitation on the scope of the action where the Legislature had not provided one. That reading follows a much older decision under the predecessor statutes, Columbia Engineering Co. v. Joiner, which said that although the proceeding is summary in nature it was not intended merely to determine technical and procedural questions involved in a corporation election, and which held that the predecessor sections provide a proceeding in equity to determine all questions that may affect the validity of a contested election.

MATTERS THE PROCEEDING WILL NOT DECIDE
The same decisions that refuse to narrow the grounds of challenge draw a boundary around the subject matter. Columbia Engineering Co. v. Joiner, immediately after holding that the predecessor sections authorize a proceeding in equity to determine all questions affecting the validity of a contested election, added that the proceeding must be limited to matters bearing on the question of the validity of the election, and that matters of corporate behavior — corporate management, general accounting, and the like — cannot be considered unless they affect that validity. Shahin v. Wawro applied that boundary. A shareholder who had purported to elect himself the sole director sued under section 709 to validate his actions and, in the same suit, to compel specific performance of an alleged agreement by the other shareholder to sell him his shares. The Court of Appeal accepted that the election question belonged in a section 709 proceeding and that such suits are equitable in nature, so that a court of equity having acquired jurisdiction will decide the entire matter; but it held that what that principle means is that all matters bearing on the question of the validity of the election will be disposed of, not everything associated with the transaction. The alleged share-sale agreements, related to the election only insofar as they might have stripped the other shareholder of voting rights, were therefore not subject to specific performance as part of the section 709 relief.

STANDING WHEN NO SHARES WERE EVER ISSUED
Corporations Code § 185 defines a “shareholder” as one who is a holder of record of shares, and that definition was the basis of the standing argument rejected in Haah v. Kim. Investors who had signed written agreements to take stock in a corporation, and who had paid in, sued under section 709 to invalidate the appointment or election of directors; the trial court found that no shares had ever been validly issued, and the defending director argued that persons who were not holders of record could not sue. The Court of Appeal held that section 709 allows persons who have entered into subscription agreements to file an action challenging the election of directors. Tracing the standing language through the predecessor statutes — where the definition of shareholder itself included a subscriber to shares when no certificates were outstanding — the court concluded that the phrase “any person who claims to have been denied the right to vote” includes those who have entered into agreements to take shares but have not yet been issued them, and reasoned that by extending standing to any person who claims to have been denied the right to vote the Legislature intended to lower the barriers to bringing the action and to let the court reach the merits without first deciding whether the plaintiff in fact had a legal right to vote.

DEFECTIVE NOTICE OF AN ADJOURNED MEETING AS A GROUND OF INVALIDITY
Spencer v. Older was a section 709 action between two families that each owned half of a corporation and each claimed the deciding board seat. A special shareholders' meeting convened without a quorum and adjourned by resolution to a time described only as just prior to, and at the same place as, the next meeting of the shareholders or directors of that corporation or of another corporation the families owned. Weeks later the meeting was reconvened and a director elected. Corporations Code § 601(d) provides that notice of an adjourned meeting need not be given if the time and place are announced at the meeting at which the adjournment is taken, and requires notice if the adjournment runs more than 45 days or a new record date is fixed. The Court of Appeal held that the meeting could not reconvene without notice, reasoning that the Legislature intended the announcement to be of a specific date and location rather than of a future event, and adding that its reading was supported by the strict construction California courts have traditionally given to notice requirements for shareholder and director meetings. On waiver, § 601(e) provides that attendance waives notice except where the person objects at the beginning of the meeting to the transaction of business because the meeting is not lawfully called or convened; the shareholders who attended under protest fell within that exception, and the court observed that neither the statute nor logic prohibits a shareholder from voting after objecting. It rejected a laches defense to a complaint filed six months after the vote, finding nothing in the record showing prejudice, and held the election conducted at the unnoticed meeting invalid.

WHO MUST BE JOINED IN THE ACTION
Section 709(b) says who must be served with the complaint and notice of the hearing, but the ordinary joinder statute also applies. Code of Civil Procedure § 389(a) requires joinder of a person subject to service whose joinder would not defeat subject matter jurisdiction where that person claims an interest relating to the subject of the action and is so situated that disposing of the action in the person's absence may impair or impede the ability to protect that interest, or may leave existing parties exposed to a substantial risk of double, multiple, or otherwise inconsistent obligations; if such a person has not been joined, the court is directed to order that the person be made a party. Morrical v. Rogers turned on that statute. The plaintiff's theory was that her two brothers, the controlling shareholders who voted in the contested election, were disqualified because they were financially self-interested in the transactions the election carried out, and the judgment invalidated both the election and transactions in which the brothers had an interest — yet the brothers were never named as parties. The Court of Appeal held that the trial court erred in failing to require their joinder, concluded that given the issues framed by the pleadings and the relief sought it was error not to require the plaintiff to join her brothers or suffer dismissal, and reversed and remanded with directions to require joinder or dismiss, without reaching the merits.

COURT ORDERS THAT AN ELECTION BE HELD AT ALL
Two other sections address the situation in which the problem is not a disputed election but the absence of one. Corporations Code § 600(c) provides that if the annual meeting is not held for 60 days after the date designated for it, or, where no date has been designated, for 15 months after the corporation was organized or after its last annual meeting, the superior court of the proper county may summarily order a meeting to be held on the application of any shareholder, after notice to the corporation giving it an opportunity to be heard. Corporations Code § 305(c) addresses a board that has filled its own vacancies: where, after such a filling, the directors then in office who were elected by the shareholders are less than a majority of the directors then in office, holders of 5 percent or more of the outstanding shares entitled to vote for those directors may call a special meeting, and the superior court shall, on application of such shareholders, summarily order a special meeting to elect the entire board, with every director's term ending on the election of a successor. The hearing on that application is held on not less than 10 business days' notice to the corporation, the corporation must file any notice of opposition no later than five business days before the hearing, the determination is made on the papers unless the court for good cause receives additional evidence, and the hearing takes precedence over other matters not of a similar nature set for that date.

A SECTION 709 CLAIM AND THE ANTI-SLAPP STATUTE
Because control fights are often already in litigation when an election is held, a section 709 claim may be met with a special motion to strike under the anti-SLAPP statute on the theory that the claim arises from the opponents' litigation conduct. In Clapkin v. Levin, a 2026 Court of Appeal decision, shareholders who claimed that shares held by a family trust should have been registered in their names pleaded a cause of action under section 709 asking the court to find their own shareholder and board meetings valid and the competing meeting invalid. The opposing side moved to strike an allegation that they were estopped from insisting on personal attendance because they had made clear, in court arguments and pleadings and elsewhere, that the shares would not be voted. The Court of Appeal reasoned that the references to court arguments and pleadings did not supply an element of the cause of action: the allegation was that the refusal had been communicated elsewhere as well, and subdivision (a) of section 709 authorizes an action by any shareholder or by any person who claims to have been denied the right to vote, so attendance at the opposing meeting was not an essential element of the claim under the statute.

The central statute is Corporations Code section 709, which directs the superior court to try and determine the validity of an election or appointment of a director in an expedited proceeding, and which sits alongside the statutes that let a court order a shareholders' meeting to be held. The sheet describes who may file such an action, how quickly it is heard, what the court may decide and order, what the published decisions have held about the grounds that may be raised and the matters that may not, and the parallel provisions that apply to nonprofit corporations. Where a specific business name appears below, that is Acme, Inc.; this sheet can also be read on its own, without it filled in, as a general reference to what these statutes and decisions say. It states the law. It does not evaluate whether any particular election was valid, whether any person holds office as a director, whether any person has standing, or what any court would decide, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

Corporations Code § 709(a) creates a civil action to test a contested board seat. Two categories of plaintiff are named: any shareholder, and any person who claims to have been denied the right to vote. The court's mandate is stated in the imperative — the superior court of the proper county “shall try and determine” the validity of any election or appointment of any director. The statute reaches every domestic corporation, and it reaches a foreign corporation as well, but only where the election was held or the appointment was made in this state. For a foreign corporation the same subdivision fixes venue at the plaintiff's option: either the county of the corporation's principal California office, or the county where the election was held or the appointment was made. The statute covers appointments as well as elections, so a directorship filled by board action rather than by a shareholder vote is within it. The section as it now reads was last amended in 2022 (Stats. 2022, ch. 617, § 17).

expectedJSON.body: Section 709(b) puts the proceeding on a short clock. On the filing of the complaint, and before any further proceedings are had, the court is to enter an order that fixes a hearing date within five days unless a later date is fixed for good cause shown, and that requires notice of the hearing date and a copy of the complaint to be served on the corporation, on the person whose purported election or appointment is questioned, and on any person other than the plaintiff whom the plaintiff alleges to have been elected or appointed; service is made as a summons is served, or by registered mail if the court so directs, and the court may impose further notice requirements as the circumstances make proper. In Morrical v. Rogers the Court of Appeal rejected the argument that this compressed schedule confines the statute to simple disputes or makes it unconstitutional to try complicated ones under it. The court read the phrase “before any further proceedings are had” as an indication that the hearing fixed by subdivision (b) is not necessarily the full trial of the complaint, and pointed out that the “good cause” clause allows a later date. In that case the complaint was filed in May 2012, the initial hearing was set for late June, and trial was held over seven days in June and July. The same opinion acknowledged that a summary trial of complex issues, conducted without the discovery and preparation available in an ordinary civil action, could deny a party procedural rights and due process.

expectedJSON.body: The decisions describe the section 709 action as equitable and as a deliberate substitute for the older remedy of quo warranto. In Lawrence v. I. N. Parlier Estate Co., decided under the predecessor provision in Civil Code section 315, the California Supreme Court said the action is in the nature of an equitable proceeding in which the court will consider all matters necessary to a proper determination of the validity of the contested election and to a just direction of the relief required. Shahin v. Wawro explained the purpose of the statute in the same terms the earlier cases had used — that courts might have power to proceed in a summary manner to test the title of directors to office without recourse to the slow and cumbersome proceeding of quo warranto — and added that the section is available to a person seeking to uphold an election as well as to one seeking to overturn it. Morrical v. Rogers stated that section 709 and its predecessor statutes afford an equitable cause of action. Quo warranto itself survives in California as Code of Civil Procedure section 803, which authorizes an action brought by the Attorney General, in the name of the people, against a person who usurps, intrudes into, or unlawfully holds or exercises a public office or a franchise, or against a corporation that does so.

expectedJSON.body: Whether a section 709 action is confined to mechanical objections — notice, quorum, vote counting — or may rest on a claim that those who controlled the vote breached their duties was the central question in Morrical v. Rogers. A minority shareholder challenged the election of new directors on the ground that her brothers, who held the controlling shares, had material financial interests in the transactions the election implemented, and the Court of Appeal held that such grounds are available: after reviewing the statute's text, its place in the code, its legislative history, and the case law, the court concluded that section 709 permits a corporate electoral challenge on those grounds. It found nothing in the plain language restricting the grounds of challenge, observed that the standing sentence of subdivision (a) limits who may sue and says nothing about the grounds, and summed up that it would not infer an unwritten limitation on the scope of the action where the Legislature had not provided one. That reading follows a much older decision under the predecessor statutes, Columbia Engineering Co. v. Joiner, which said that although the proceeding is summary in nature it was not intended merely to determine technical and procedural questions involved in a corporation election, and which held that the predecessor sections provide a proceeding in equity to determine all questions that may affect the validity of a contested election.

nothing in the plain language of section 709 restricts the grounds on which the validity of an election or appointment of directors can be challenged
However, the plain language restricts only standing to bring an action and says nothing about the grounds on which persons with standing may challenge the validity of an election.
In sum, we find no basis to infer an unwritten limitation on the scope of an action under section 709 where the Legislature has not expressly provided for such a limitation.

A review of these indicates that although summary in nature, the actions provided for by it were not intended to be, as contended by defendants, merely to determine technical and procedural questions involved in a corporation election.

We hold that sections 2236-2238, Corporations Code, providing as they do for a proceeding in equity to determine all questions which may affect the validity of a contested election, authorize the action here brought.

expectedJSON.body: The same decisions that refuse to narrow the grounds of challenge draw a boundary around the subject matter. Columbia Engineering Co. v. Joiner, immediately after holding that the predecessor sections authorize a proceeding in equity to determine all questions affecting the validity of a contested election, added that the proceeding must be limited to matters bearing on the question of the validity of the election, and that matters of corporate behavior — corporate management, general accounting, and the like — cannot be considered unless they affect that validity. Shahin v. Wawro applied that boundary. A shareholder who had purported to elect himself the sole director sued under section 709 to validate his actions and, in the same suit, to compel specific performance of an alleged agreement by the other shareholder to sell him his shares. The Court of Appeal accepted that the election question belonged in a section 709 proceeding and that such suits are equitable in nature, so that a court of equity having acquired jurisdiction will decide the entire matter; but it held that what that principle means is that all matters bearing on the question of the validity of the election will be disposed of, not everything associated with the transaction. The alleged share-sale agreements, related to the election only insofar as they might have stripped the other shareholder of voting rights, were therefore not subject to specific performance as part of the section 709 relief.

The alleged agreements of Wawro to sell his shares to Shahin, not being related to the latter’s purported election except insofar as they might have deprived Wawro of his voting rights, were therefore not subject to specific performance as part of Shahin’s request for relief under section 709.

expectedJSON.body: Corporations Code § 185 defines a “shareholder” as one who is a holder of record of shares, and that definition was the basis of the standing argument rejected in Haah v. Kim. Investors who had signed written agreements to take stock in a corporation, and who had paid in, sued under section 709 to invalidate the appointment or election of directors; the trial court found that no shares had ever been validly issued, and the defending director argued that persons who were not holders of record could not sue. The Court of Appeal held that section 709 allows persons who have entered into subscription agreements to file an action challenging the election of directors. Tracing the standing language through the predecessor statutes — where the definition of shareholder itself included a subscriber to shares when no certificates were outstanding — the court concluded that the phrase “any person who claims to have been denied the right to vote” includes those who have entered into agreements to take shares but have not yet been issued them, and reasoned that by extending standing to any person who claims to have been denied the right to vote the Legislature intended to lower the barriers to bringing the action and to let the court reach the merits without first deciding whether the plaintiff in fact had a legal right to vote.

expectedJSON.body: Spencer v. Older was a section 709 action between two families that each owned half of a corporation and each claimed the deciding board seat. A special shareholders' meeting convened without a quorum and adjourned by resolution to a time described only as just prior to, and at the same place as, the next meeting of the shareholders or directors of that corporation or of another corporation the families owned. Weeks later the meeting was reconvened and a director elected. Corporations Code § 601(d) provides that notice of an adjourned meeting need not be given if the time and place are announced at the meeting at which the adjournment is taken, and requires notice if the adjournment runs more than 45 days or a new record date is fixed. The Court of Appeal held that the meeting could not reconvene without notice, reasoning that the Legislature intended the announcement to be of a specific date and location rather than of a future event, and adding that its reading was supported by the strict construction California courts have traditionally given to notice requirements for shareholder and director meetings. On waiver, § 601(e) provides that attendance waives notice except where the person objects at the beginning of the meeting to the transaction of business because the meeting is not lawfully called or convened; the shareholders who attended under protest fell within that exception, and the court observed that neither the statute nor logic prohibits a shareholder from voting after objecting. It rejected a laches defense to a complaint filed six months after the vote, finding nothing in the record showing prejudice, and held the election conducted at the unnoticed meeting invalid.

expectedJSON.body: Section 709(b) says who must be served with the complaint and notice of the hearing, but the ordinary joinder statute also applies. Code of Civil Procedure § 389(a) requires joinder of a person subject to service whose joinder would not defeat subject matter jurisdiction where that person claims an interest relating to the subject of the action and is so situated that disposing of the action in the person's absence may impair or impede the ability to protect that interest, or may leave existing parties exposed to a substantial risk of double, multiple, or otherwise inconsistent obligations; if such a person has not been joined, the court is directed to order that the person be made a party. Morrical v. Rogers turned on that statute. The plaintiff's theory was that her two brothers, the controlling shareholders who voted in the contested election, were disqualified because they were financially self-interested in the transactions the election carried out, and the judgment invalidated both the election and transactions in which the brothers had an interest — yet the brothers were never named as parties. The Court of Appeal held that the trial court erred in failing to require their joinder, concluded that given the issues framed by the pleadings and the relief sought it was error not to require the plaintiff to join her brothers or suffer dismissal, and reversed and remanded with directions to require joinder or dismiss, without reaching the merits.

expectedJSON.body: Section 709 sits in the General Corporation Law. The Nonprofit Corporation Law carries its own versions. For a nonprofit public benefit corporation, Corporations Code § 5617(a) directs the superior court, on the filing of an action by any director or member, or by any person who had the right to vote in the election at issue, to determine the validity of any election or appointment of any director; subdivision (b) requires any person bringing such an action to give notice to the Attorney General, who may intervene. For a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation, § 7616(a) is worded the same way as to who may sue, and § 7616(b) requires notice to the Attorney General only where the corporation holds assets in charitable trust. Section 7616(d) directs the court, consistent with that part and in conformity with the articles and bylaws to the extent feasible, to determine the person entitled to the office, order a new election or appointment, determine the validity, effectiveness and construction of voting agreements and voting trusts, the validity of the issuance of memberships, and the right of persons to vote, and to direct such other relief as may be just and proper. That the general statute does not stretch to cover other corporation types was the point of Stevens v. Perkins, where directors of a church corporation organized under the former General Nonprofit Corporation Law petitioned under section 709: the Court of Appeal held a cause of action based on the new section 709 was precluded, and that the petition could be amended to state a cause of action under the former Corporations Code sections 2236-2238, which it concluded had continuing application to nonprofit corporations despite their repeal.

expectedJSON.body: Two other sections address the situation in which the problem is not a disputed election but the absence of one. Corporations Code § 600(c) provides that if the annual meeting is not held for 60 days after the date designated for it, or, where no date has been designated, for 15 months after the corporation was organized or after its last annual meeting, the superior court of the proper county may summarily order a meeting to be held on the application of any shareholder, after notice to the corporation giving it an opportunity to be heard. At a meeting so ordered, the shares represented and entitled to vote constitute a quorum notwithstanding any contrary provision in the articles, the bylaws, or the division itself, and the court may issue appropriate orders including orders fixing the time and place, the record date, and the form of notice. Corporations Code § 305(c) addresses a board that has filled its own vacancies: where, after such a filling, the directors then in office who were elected by the shareholders are less than a majority of the directors then in office, holders of 5 percent or more of the outstanding shares entitled to vote for those directors may call a special meeting, and the superior court shall, on application of such shareholders, summarily order a special meeting to elect the entire board, with every director's term ending on the election of a successor. The hearing on that application is held on not less than 10 business days' notice to the corporation, the corporation must file any notice of opposition no later than five business days before the hearing, the determination is made on the papers unless the court for good cause receives additional evidence, and the hearing takes precedence over other matters not of a similar nature set for that date.

In Clapkin v. Levin, a 2026 Court of Appeal decision, shareholders who claimed that shares held by a family trust should have been registered in their names pleaded a cause of action under section 709 asking the court to find their own shareholder and board meetings valid and the competing meeting invalid. The opposing side moved to strike an allegation that they were estopped from insisting on personal attendance because they had made clear, in court arguments and pleadings and elsewhere, that the shares would not be voted. The Court of Appeal reasoned that the references to court arguments and pleadings did not supply an element of the cause of action: the allegation was that the refusal had been communicated elsewhere as well, and subdivision (a) of section 709 authorizes an action by any shareholder or by any person who claims to have been denied the right to vote, so attendance at the opposing meeting was not an essential element of the claim under the statute.
